body.text: Surging threat of white nationalist terror prompts call to drop 'religion' from terrorism definition
In short:
The national security watchdog is urging the government to change the way it defines terrorism to exclude the word religion.
It argues the current definition causes harm to groups like Australia's Muslim community.
Police and security agencies have previously warned against a change.
The federal government is being urged to rethink how it defines terrorism to better reflect growing racist and white nationalist threats, and drop references to religion.

The contentious proposal has been made by the government's independent national security legislation monitor (INSLM), Jake Blight, who argues changing the definition would simplify legal processes and help prosecute terror threats.

But the idea generated pushback before the recommendation was even formally made, with some national security analysts suggesting the change would diminish "openness about motivation" in terror cases.
The current definition of terrorism requires proving a motivation to "advance a political, religious or ideological cause".
Mr Blight's 15-month review, tabled in the Senate this afternoon, recommended dumping religion from that test, and broadening the definition of "ideology" to capture religious motives.

He pointed to difficulties prosecuting some terror cases to argue his point — noting that ISIS-inspired terror cases had an 84 per cent conviction rate, while those with racist or nationalist ideologies were only convicted in half of all cases.
He argued the changes he was suggesting would help those non-ISIS cases fare better once they got to court.
"I think the change in relation to ideology will make prosecuting easier," he said.
"It will provide a solid basis for this growing cohort of other ideologies.
"The change in religion will not make it any more difficult or any different for police and how they prosecute those cases."
The federal government has previously indicated some reluctance to remove "religion" from the definition of terrorism.
Asked about dumping terrorism from the definition earlier this week, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was quick to say it was not on the table.
"The prime minister's already made clear that a change like that is not something that we would make," he said.
However, following the release of the review, Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said the government would deliberate the findings.
"We thank the INSLM for their work on its own-motion review, as well as the organisations and individuals who engaged in this review," she said.
"The government will carefully consider the recommendations and provide a formal response in due course.
"The government is committed to ensuring the definition of terrorism is sufficiently broad to respond to current and future threats."

Mr Blight said the change had been wrongly viewed by some as narrowing the definition, and urged the government to fully the "complex and detailed" report, following 15 months of extensive consultation.
Religious definition 'not doing us any good'
Agencies like the Australian Federal Police and domestic security agency ASIO have cautioned against changes to the definition, warning of unintended consequences.
In a submission to the review, the AFP said the current definition was "robust and effective", and had been "well tested in Australian courts over many years".
Mr Blight said there was also a strong view among some groups that religiously-motivated terror should be "called for what it is".
But he said he came to the view that changing the definition wouldn't change how police and security agencies approach their task.
"I think police and ASIO are very capable of internally describing the crimes however they see them," he said.
"We don't set it in our law for them, they're very smart, they can work this out. This change will not affect how they prosecute, how they investigate, how they call things internally."

The idea to drop religion from the definition of terrorism was supported by some Muslim groups, including the Australian Federation of Islamic Councils, which argued it had discriminatory consequences.
"It has legitimised suspicion of Islamic religious identity, enabled profiling and overreach, and fundamentally undermined trust in public institutions and the rule of law," it said in a submission.
AFIC called for the "motive" element of the terrorism definition to be dropped altogether, replaced with a focus on conduct and intent, without reference to ideology at all.
Mr Blight said that approach risked broadening the definition of terrorism much too far.
"It would dilute counterterrorism resources," he said.
"And it would bring crimes that don't need the special terrorism framework, like organised crime, gang crime, into this specialised terrorism framework."
But he agreed including religion in the definition of terrorism was doing harm to groups like the Muslim community.
He said keeping religion in the definition risked giving terrorists from groups like ISIL the validation they sought — as belonging to a religious cause.
"They want to be recognised as religious warriors. And when we recognise them in law as advancing a religious cause, we're giving them what they want," he said.
"We're giving them false credibility and a recruitment platform that, frankly, I don't think they deserve.
"We should still prosecute them, we can still prosecute them, we should jail them as violent ideologues and not give them that credibility."
Calls for youth radicalisation inquiry
Mr Blight also used the new report to raise the alarm on youth radicalisation, warning the surge in cases warranted significant public inquiry.
He pointed to recent caseload figures suggesting two-thirds of all those charged with terrorism offences so far this year were children, up from 8 per cent only a few years ago.
The issue has been frequently raised in recent months, with the Australian Federal Police among those sounding alarm at the rising youth caseload.
"I think we need a review that looks at three broad areas. First of all, why are so many children going down the path of extremism towards violence? What can we do at that very early stage?" he said.

"Second, there's questions about online radicalisation. The vast majority of these children are from families that have no connection to terrorism, no history of terrorism. They're radicalised alone online. So we need to look at that online space.

"And then thirdly, we absolutely need police to protect us when children are violent. Children can commit terrorism. But we also need to look at are our laws, which were really drafted with adults in mind, fit for purpose for children?"
